opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of those results that really jumped out at me. When John Hewitt and Chris Manning published their structural probe, they found that if you take BERT's contextual embeddings and apply a linear transformation, the distance between two words in the parse tree corresponds to the *squared* Euclidean distance between their transformed vectors. Not the ordinary distance, the squared one. And my first reaction was: why squared? That seemed strange. If you were designing it, you'd expect plain distance.

So we started thinking about it mathematically, and it turns out there's a lovely, simple explanation. If you try to embed a tree in Euclidean space so that ordinary distance matches tree distance, you quickly run into trouble. Trees branch, and you just can't make that work isometrically in general. But if you ask for *squared* distance to match tree distance, it suddenly becomes easy.

Here's the construction. Pick the root and put it at the origin. Then, for every edge in the tree, assign its own unit vector, with all those vectors mutually orthogonal. Each node's position is the sum of the edge vectors along the path from the root down to it. Now take any two nodes. The difference between their positions is a sum of unit vectors for exactly the edges on the path between them, and since those vectors are all orthogonal, the Pythagorean theorem says the squared length of that difference is just the number of edges. That's exactly tree distance.

We started calling these "Pythagorean embeddings." What struck me is that this isn't some contrived trick. It's arguably the most natural way to put a tree into a high-dimensional vector space, and these networks have plenty of dimensions to work with. So the squared-distance finding stopped looking like a weird coincidence and started looking like evidence that the model might be doing something quite sensible geometrically.

Then, being a visualization person, I wanted to actually see it. We took the probed embeddings for real sentences and compared them to what an ideal Pythagorean embedding of the parse tree would look like. The broad shapes matched surprisingly well. You could also see systematic deviations, which were interesting in their own right, because they hinted that the model's representation of syntax isn't a perfect copy of a textbook parse tree. It's encoding something richer or slightly different.

For me, the bigger lesson was about interpretability in general. Sometimes an empirical finding looks puzzling, and a little bit of math tells you that it's actually the natural answer. That pairing of a clean theoretical lens with a visualization that lets you check it against reality is something I find really powerful.

r001.rationale: The response says tree distances cannot generally be matched isometrically by ordinary Euclidean distances because trees branch.

r002.rationale: It assigns mutually orthogonal unit vectors to tree edges, places each node at the sum along its root path, and explains that the squared distance equals the number of edges between nodes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it started as a genuine puzzle. When John Hewitt and Chris Manning published that structural probe paper, the headline result was that you could find a linear transformation of BERT's embeddings such that the distance between two word vectors corresponds to the distance between those words in the parse tree. And that's already remarkable. But the detail that nagged at us was that it wasn't the Euclidean distance that matched tree distance. It was the squared Euclidean distance. And if you're a geometer, that's a strange thing to see, because squared distance isn't a metric in the usual sense. It doesn't even satisfy the triangle inequality. So why would that be the quantity that lines up?

So we spent a while just staring at it, and the way we eventually made sense of it was to ask a simpler question. Forget neural networks for a second. If you wanted to embed a tree into Euclidean space so that squared distance equals tree distance, could you do it at all? And it turns out you can, and the construction is almost embarrassingly simple. You put the root at the origin, and then every edge in the tree gets its own orthogonal unit direction. To embed a node, you walk from the root and add up the unit vectors for each edge along the way. Now if you take two nodes and look at the difference between their embeddings, the shared part of their paths cancels out, and what's left is a sum of orthogonal unit vectors, one for each edge on the path between them. The squared length of that is just the number of edges. So squared distance equals path length, exactly.

Once you see that, the squared Euclidean distance stops looking like an accident and starts looking almost forced. Trees want to be embedded this way. It's a kind of Pythagorean construction, where every branch is a right turn away from everything else. And it also tells you why plain Euclidean distance wouldn't work in general. If you want ordinary distance to match path length, you're asking for the tree to lie along geodesics, which fails as soon as you have a branching node with three or more children. You'd need all the children to be collinear and that's impossible.

The other thing that fell out of this, which I found quite beautiful, is that the construction isn't unique. You have a lot of freedom in choosing those orthogonal directions, and in fact you can relax it. We ended up calling these power-p embeddings, where you ask that the distance to the p-th power match tree distance. And it turns out that p equals 2 is a kind of boundary. For p less than 2 you can still find embeddings but the structure is different, and for p greater than 2 things get more constrained. So the fact that BERT seems to land right at p equals 2 is suggestive. It's the case where you get this clean, simple, orthogonal-edge geometry.

And then of course the natural next step was to go look. We took the actual BERT embeddings, projected them using Hewitt and Manning's probe, and visualized them, and you really do see tree-like structures that resemble this idealized construction, though noisier and with some systematic distortions. For instance, certain dependency types seemed to have consistently longer or shorter edges than the ideal. So the model isn't producing the textbook embedding, but it's producing something that rhymes with it. And for me that was the satisfying part, that a piece of pure geometry gave us a lens for interpreting what was otherwise just a surprising empirical regularity.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary Euclidean distance cannot match tree path length in general, explaining that a branching node with three or more children would require its children to be collinear.

r002.rationale: It describes assigning each tree edge its own orthogonal direction, summing those directions from the root, and shows that the squared distance between nodes equals the number of edges on their path.

astra-6.text:
The way I made sense of it was to imagine giving every edge in the tree its own perpendicular direction. Put the root at the origin, and position each node by adding up the unit vectors for the edges on the path from the root to that node.

Now take two nodes. The parts of their paths that they share cancel out when you subtract their vectors. What’s left is one unit vector, with a plus or minus sign, for each edge on the path between them. Since those directions are perpendicular, the Pythagorean theorem tells you that the squared Euclidean distance is exactly the number of edges on that path.

So the square actually makes sense: any tree admits that kind of representation. That doesn’t explain why a language model learns something a linear probe can recover, but it gives you a clean geometric picture of what the probe is looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says the squared Euclidean distance equals the path length and that any tree admits this representation; it does not state that ordinary Euclidean distances cannot generally represent tree distances exactly.

r002.rationale: It describes assigning each tree edge its own perpendicular unit direction and explains that the squared distance between nodes equals the number of edges on their path.
